item.title: Data Center Expansion in Texas Risks Reversing Decades of Air Quality Gains
item.description:
Data Center Expansion in Texas Risks Reversing Decades of Air Quality Gains

New research from the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC) indicates that a surge of data centers in Texas could return air pollution to levels not seen since the 2000s. As Texas becomes a primary hub for generative AI infrastructure, the massive electricity demands of these facilities threaten to erase decades of air quality progress.

⚙️ Key details

Texas currently leads the data center market with 26 gigawatts of existing and under-construction capacity. According to a March Wood Mackenzie report, Texas is also preparing for four times more proposed data center capacity running on onsite power generation than any other state.

💡 Why it matters

The environmental impact depends on how developers and utilities meet electricity demands. A HARC report warns that if all planned projects use the anticipated grid mix, the results could be severe:

  • Fine particle pollution (soot): Could more than triple, reaching the highest level since 2006.
  • Smog-forming NOx emissions: Could increase 136 percent, approaching 2004 levels.
  • Carbon dioxide pollution: Could climb 90 percent above 2025 levels.

John Hall, HARC CEO, stated, “There is a good chance that our children and grandchildren will breathe dirtier air than we did,” adding that progress made by the state, the transportation sector, and other stakeholders is now at risk.

🧩 How it works

The level of pollution is determined by the power sources chosen by developers:

Power Source Environmental Impact
Onsite Renewables NOx emissions could be up to 10 times lower when paired with grid power.
Grid Mix High levels of soot and smog-forming pollutants.
Onsite Gas Engines Potential for the highest pollution levels possible; often used to avoid grid connection wait times.
Gas Turbines Less efficient technology used to speed construction, increasing pollution.

#Texas #DataCenters #AirPollution #GenerativeAI #EnergyInfrastructure

Source: Data centers could erase decades of air quality gains

item.title: Basel Action Network Predicts AI Will Significantly Increase Global E-Waste
item.description:
Basel Action Network Predicts AI Will Significantly Increase Global E-Waste

The nonprofit Basel Action Network (BAN) published a paper today predicting that AI will contribute significantly to the growth of global electronic waste through 2050.

⚙️ Key details

BAN predicts global e-waste will triple to 211 million metric tons per year by 2050, attributing 15 to 20 percent of that garbage to AI. The organization’s findings include:

  • Estimated AI Waste: Between 2025 and 2050, AI-related electronic equipment is expected to add between 395 to 617 million metric tons of e-waste.
  • Annual Impact: This breaks down to approximately 8.6 million to 13.1 million metric tons of equipment retired annually due to AI.
  • Data Center Capacity: BAN expects 70,000 metric tons of e-waste per gigawatt of data center capacity. It cites a McKinsey projection that total capacity could reach 219GW by 2030.
  • Scope of Waste: BAN includes power supply and distribution, cooling systems, backup power, and networking equipment, noting that studies focusing only on servers and accelerators miss about 87 percent of a data center’s electro-mechanical infrastructure.
  • AI Waste Contagion: This category includes telecommunications infrastructure and personal devices that may be replaced earlier due to AI advances.

💡 Why it matters

Currently, less than a quarter of the 68.3 million tons of e-waste created annually worldwide is formally collected and recycled. Most e-waste ends up in “informal” collection where burying or burning equipment exposes workers and the environment to toxic materials such as chromium and lead.

By 2050, the volume of waste could be enough to fill 23 million shipping containers, which would circle the world six times if lined up. BAN notes that the US has more data centers than any other country but has not ratified the Basel Convention intended to limit the international trade of hazardous wastes; investigations have found US recyclers still ship e-waste abroad, where it often enters “backyard recycling.”

#AI #e-waste #Sustainability #BaselActionNetwork #DataCenters

Source: The AI data center e-waste problem is huge — and getting bigger
